You're designing a part for someone to 3D print at home. They'll print it on their own printer, use only the hardware listed below, and put it together by following your manual.

## Their setup
- Printer: Bambu Lab X1C (with AMS), build volume 256 x 256 x 256 mm
- Nozzle: 0.4 mm
- Layer height: 0.2 mm
- Filament: PLA (high-speed PLA, black)
- Longest bridge seen to print cleanly on this setup: 50 mm

## Hardware they can use
Refer to an item by its catalog reference: "ISO 4762 M5x30" (socket head screw, size x length, from the lengths listed), "ISO 4032 M5" (hex nut), "ISO 10511 M5" (nylon-insert lock nut), "ISO 7089 M5" (washer), "ASME B18.2.2 1/4-20" (1/4"-20 nut), "insert M3x4x5" (heat-set insert), "salvaged:webcam-mount-bolt".

## How to work
You have these tools:
- measure(item, what): ask the person to measure one of their own things, such as their desk or their phone. They answer with what they measured, or say they can't measure it.
- submit_design(...): hand in the finished design. This ends the conversation.
- report_limitation(wanted, blocked_by, why): say you wanted to use something (a technique, a tool, a part or material, a way of handing in the design) but couldn't because of what's available here. It doesn't change anything, but it's noted.
You have at most 8 turns. Hand in a design before they run out.

## The design you hand in
submit_design's schema describes every field. The rules that matter:
- Every dimension that comes from hardware or the real world is a named param, with its source: measured (the person measured it for you), datasheet, catalog, asked (the person told you), guessed, unknown, or design (your own choice).
- Each part's `code` is Python that defines build(p) and returns a CadQuery Workplane or Shape. `cq` is already imported, and p.<name> is each param's value. Dimensions that come from hardware or the real world must come from params.
- Model each part in the orientation it's printed in, with z = 0 on the bed.
- The manual is the steps the person follows, naming the parts and hardware each step uses.
I need a round spacer to go on an M5 bolt between two plates. Make it 20 mm long and 12 mm across, with a clearance hole for the bolt.
A simple part — a 20 × 12 mm round spacer with an M5 clearance hole. Before I pick the bolt length, let me check the two plates it's sandwiching, so the bolt is the right size.

Simple design: a cylinder 20 mm long, 12 mm OD, M5 clearance hole (5.5 mm hole for M5 bolt). Print orientation: on end. Use socket head screw ISO 4762 M5x... length? The bolt is their own M5 bolt? They said "an M5 bolt" — maybe it's theirs. But hardware list has M5 screws. Length needed: 20 mm spacer + two plates. We don't know plate thickness. Hmm. Could ask, but we have 8 turns. The joint spec — maybe we just include a bolt of appropriate length. Plate thicknesses unknown. We could ask them to measure plates, or just report limitation. Simpler: ask one measure call for plate thicknesses? The task is just the spacer; but joint info requires hardware seats. We could define the joint with external? The bolt threads into... it's a through-bolt with nut. Joint: fastener M5x?? seats: spacer clearance, plate1 clearance, plate2 clearance, nut pocket with ISO 4032 M5.

We don't know plate thicknesses. Options: ask via measure tool. One call: "plate thickness (both plates)". Then compute bolt length: spacer 20 + plates + nut. Min threaded engagement... Actually let's just ask. Or submit with a guess and note. Better to measure: "the two plates" thickness each. Let's make two measure calls in parallel: plate1 thickness, plate2 thickness.

Then compute: bolt length ≥ 20 + t1 + t2 + washer(1) + nut(4.7) + ~2 mm. Round up to available lengths: 30,35,40,45,50.

Design: cylinder OD 12, height 20, hole d 5.5 through. Chamfer ends maybe 0.5. Print orientation: flat end on bed, no supports needed.

Params: spacer_od=12 (asked), spacer_len=20 (asked), clearance_d=5.5 (design), t1, t2 measured, bolt length design choice.

Add chamfer: .edges().chamfer(0.6)? Chamfer on top/bottom edges of cylinder—hole edge too. Fine, small chamfer 0.5 on outer edges only; hole chamfer helps insertion. Simpler: chamfer all circular edges 0.5.

Print orientation: "cylindrical face down" — lying on side? Printing a tube on end wastes little material and no supports needed for the hole; but a 20 tall 12 dia on end prints fine (small contact area, could use brim). Lying on side, the hole is horizontal — bridging top of hole over 5.5 mm span, fine, but surface roughness. On end is fine; the hole prints perfectly. Recommend on end with brim/raft. Use_orientation: print flat end on bed.

They can't measure the plates, so I'll pick a bolt length that covers a sensible range of plate thicknesses and make that explicit. The spacer itself is straightforward: Ø12 × 20 mm with a Ø5.5 mm through-hole (standard M5 close-fit clearance), chamfered hole entries so the bolt slides in, printed standing on end so the bore comes out perfectly round with no bridging.

I'll include a tiny test disc (same hole, 5 mm thick) as a coupon so they can check the bolt slips through before printing the real part.
reasoning:
They can't measure. So pick a conservative bolt length that covers typical plates. Spacer 20 + washer 1.0 + nut 4.7 ≈ 25.7 mm before plates. Available lengths: 25, 30, 35... If I choose M5x30, that leaves ~4.3 mm for two plates — too thin. M5x35 leaves ~9.3 mm for plates. Hmm, guessing plate thicknesses: typical sheet metal 2-3 mm, plywood 6-10 mm, 3D-printed plates 4-8 mm.

I'll guess plates ~4 mm each (typical printed or sheet plates): 20 + 4 + 4 = 28, + washer 1 + nut 4.7 = 33.7 → M5x35 gives ~1.3 mm of thread past the nut, marginal. M5x40 gives 6.3 mm spare. Overshoot means the bolt sticks out, which is fine (spacer still works, bolt protrudes past nut).

Better approach: make the spacer the exact requested size and choose bolt length to fit a range: M5x40 covers plates up to ~9 mm each (20+9+9=38, +1+4.7=43.7, slightly over... 40 works for plates totaling ≤13.3 mm). Hmm: bolt 40, spacer 20, washer 1, nut 4.7 → plates total ≤ 14.3 mm for the nut to fully engage (need full nut height engagement: threads past plates ≥ 4.7). If plates are thinner, bolt sticks out more — harmless unless they care about cosmetics.

Actually wait — do I even need the bolt? They said "on an M5 bolt" — they may already have the bolt. The salvaged webcam-mount-bolt is 1/4-20, not M5. They said M5 bolt, so hardware list has ISO 4762 M5 screws. I'll include an M5x40 socket screw, washer, and lock nut in the hardware and design the joint. But if they already have a bolt, extra hardware is harmless — I'll note it in the manual: "if your existing M5 bolt is long enough, use it."

Hmm, but joint spec: bolt through spacer (clearance), plate1 clearance, plate2 clearance, then lock nut on end (nut_pocket — the nut is external on the threads; role nut_pocket? For a bolt+nut joint, the nut seat on the last part. I'll list seats: spacer clearance, plate1 clearance, plate2 clearance, and the nut as nut_pocket on... nut isn't seated in a part here. I can make joint with seats for the three clearances and set nut to the lock nut hardware id. The lock nut provides thread engagement on the end of the bolt.

Bolt length choice: I'll go M5x40 as a robust default for unknown plates (covers plate totals 5–14 mm). Note in params: plate thickness unknown/guessed.

- Spacer: OD 12 mm, length 20 mm, through hole Ø5.5 mm (M5 clearance, close fit ~5.5). Chamfer both hole entries 0.5 mm for easy insertion, and small chamfer on ends.
- Print standing on end (flat face down): hole is axial, prints clean, no supports. With a 12 mm contact area, add brim in slicer (manual note). PLA. Print_orientation: "flat end face down (hole axis vertical)". Use_orientation: "hole axis vertical (same as printed)".

Wait — on-end printing of a 12 mm × 20 mm tube: small bed contact, but fine with brim. Alternative: lying on side, hole horizontal — top of hole is a 5.5 mm bridge, trivial, but oval hole and rough surface. On end is better.

Criteria: hole clears M5 screw with 0.5 mm clearance; OD/length as asked. Coupon? Could print a small coupon to check the hole — a 12 mm dia × 4 mm disc with 5.5 hole is itself basically a test. I could make the spacer itself the check via "measure" method. Keep criteria: hole_d clears bolt (method: measure the printed hole or just measure; check method 'coupon' — print one spacer as coupon? It's tiny anyway; printing one spacer first to verify bolt fit is sensible. I'll add a coupon part: same geometry scaled? Simpler: role coupon part "spacer_fit_test" — a 5 mm thick disc 12 mm OD with the 5.5 hole, to test bolt slip-fit before printing the final 20 mm one. That's a nice touch and cheap.

Parts:
1. spacer (final): cyl 12 OD × 20, hole 5.5, chamfers.
2. spacer_fit_coupon: 12 OD × 5 thick disc with 5.5 hole — same print orientation; test bolt passes through.

Hardware: ISO 4762 M5x40 (qty 1), ISO 10511 M5 lock nut (qty 1), ISO 7089 M5 washer (qty 1).

Joint: id "spacer-bolt-joint", fastener m5x40, axis origin (0,0,0) at spacer bottom face center? Axis origin is where the head sits in frame of first seat part. First seat: spacer clearance... Actually head sits on plate1? Order: head → plate1 → spacer → plate2 → nut? They said spacer between two plates. Head on plate 1, washer, spacer, plate 2, washer?, lock nut. Washer under head. I'll put washer under head and under nut.

Joint frame: first part in seats = plate1? But plates aren't parts of this design. Hmm — plates aren't in `parts`. Seats must reference parts. The plates aren't printable parts here. Can seats reference external things? `external` field is for outside the design (e.g., camera socket). The plates are external too. But seats require part ids of parts. Maybe I only list the spacer's clearance seat, and use external for plates+nut? Nut goes on the bolt, external nut isn't a seat in a part either.

Simplest valid: joint with seats: [spacer clearance], external: "the two plates and the lock nut" — external is "anything outside the design it threads into". The bolt doesn't thread into the spacer; it threads into the lock nut which is hardware... The nut is in hardware list. Hmm, joint.nut field: "id of an item in hardware". So: seats: spacer clearance (plus coupon not in joint), nut: lock_nut id, external: "the two 4-ish mm plates the bolt clamps (thickness unmeasured)".

Axis origin in spacer frame: hole center at (0,0,0)? Head sits below the spacer on plate1. In the spacer's own frame, origin at bottom face center, direction +Z (head to tip = upward through spacer). OK: axis_origin [0,0,-25]? "Where the fastener's head sits, in the frame of the first part in seats". Spacer frame z=0 bottom, z=20 top. Head is below z=0. Put origin [0,0,-1] (washer under head)... it's fine: [0,0,-2], dir [0,0,1].

Code for spacer:

def build(p):
    return (cq.Workplane("XY")
        .circle(p.spacer_od/2)
        .extrude(p.spacer_len)
        .faces(">Z").workplane()
        .hole(p.hole_d)
        .edges("%CIRCLE").chamfer(p.chamfer))

Careful: edges("%CIRCLE") after hole selects circular edges including hole edges — chamfer 0.5 on hole edges gives lead-in. Good. But chamfering both ends' hole edges: edges("%CIRCLE") picks all circular edges (outer rims at z=0 and z=20, hole rims). Chamfer 0.5 might fail on 5.5 hole? No, fine.

2. Print spacer.
3. Assembly: washer on bolt, head... order: bolt head + washer → plate1 → spacer → plate2 → washer → lock nut; tighten. If their own bolt: any M5 ≥ ~28 mm for 4 mm plates... note bolt length logic.

- spacer length = 20: criterion "spacer height is 20 mm", relation supports? These criteria need part+feature+relation. I'll do: {part spacer, feature bore, relation clears, hardware m5x40, clearance 0.5, check coupon}; {part spacer, feature outer cylinder, relation contains, ...} eh. Keep it minimal but sensible: one for hole clearance, one for length/OD as-asked (check: measure).

They can't measure. So pick a conservative bolt length that covers typical plates. Spacer 20 + washer 1.0 + nut 4.7 ≈ 25.7 mm before plates. Available lengths: 25, 30, 35... If I choose M5x30, that leaves ~4.3 mm for two plates — too thin. M5x35 leaves ~9.3 mm for plates. Hmm, guessing plate thicknesses: typical sheet metal 2-3 mm, plywood 6-10 mm, 3D-printed plates 4-8 mm.

I'll guess plates ~4 mm each (typical printed or sheet plates): 20 + 4 + 4 = 28, + washer 1 + nut 4.7 = 33.7 → M5x35 gives ~1.3 mm of thread past the nut, marginal. M5x40 gives 6.3 mm spare. Overshoot means the bolt sticks out, which is fine (spacer still works, bolt protrudes past nut).

Better approach: make the spacer the exact requested size and choose bolt length to fit a range: M5x40 covers plates up to ~9 mm each (20+9+9=38, +1+4.7=43.7, slightly over... 40 works for plates totaling ≤13.3 mm). Hmm: bolt 40, spacer 20, washer 1, nut 4.7 → plates total ≤ 14.3 mm for the nut to fully engage (need full nut height engagement: threads past plates ≥ 4.7). If plates are thinner, bolt sticks out more — harmless unless they care about cosmetics.

Actually wait — do I even need the bolt? They said "on an M5 bolt" — they may already have the bolt. The salvaged webcam-mount-bolt is 1/4-20, not M5. They said M5 bolt, so hardware list has ISO 4762 M5 screws. I'll include an M5x40 socket screw, washer, and lock nut in the hardware and design the joint. But if they already have a bolt, extra hardware is harmless — I'll note it in the manual: "if your existing M5 bolt is long enough, use it."

Hmm, but joint spec: bolt through spacer (clearance), plate1 clearance, plate2 clearance, then lock nut on end (nut_pocket — the nut is external on the threads; role nut_pocket? For a bolt+nut joint, the nut seat on the last part. I'll list seats: spacer clearance, plate1 clearance, plate2 clearance, and the nut as nut_pocket on... nut isn't seated in a part here. I can make joint with seats for the three clearances and set nut to the lock nut hardware id. The lock nut provides thread engagement on the end of the bolt.

Bolt length choice: I'll go M5x40 as a robust default for unknown plates (covers plate totals 5–14 mm). Note in params: plate thickness unknown/guessed.

Wait — on-end printing of a 12 mm × 20 mm tube: small bed contact, but fine with brim. Alternative: lying on side, hole horizontal — top of hole is a 5.5 mm bridge, trivial, but oval hole and rough surface. On end is better.
